header.name: Computational Complexity Theory
header.description: One of the many beautiful results in the theory of computation is the equivalence of “deterministic” and “non-deterministic” variants of different models of computation, like Turing machines. One may ask whether this equivalence holds if we restrict the running time (or number of steps) of a Turing machine. This gives rise to one of the most important open problems in computer science, popularly known as the ‘P versus NP’ question. This will be the starting point of our course. After briefly recalling Turing machines and discussing formal definitions of the classes ‘P’ and ‘NP’, we will see the notion of ‘reductions’, which will allow us to talk about the ‘hardest’ problems in NP, known as NP-complete problems. We will discuss some important NP-complete problems from different areas, like logic, graph theory, etc. After that, we will briefly talk about other important classes corresponding to the running time of a Turing machine, like ‘co-NP’, ‘EXP’, and ‘NEXP’. Following this, we will see a classification of computational problems based on the space used by the Turing machine. We will discuss some important classes like PSPACE and NPSPACE (the space-variants of P and NP, respectively), L and NL (the log-space versions of P and NP), their relations with P and NP, a ‘PSPACE-complete’ problem, the equivalence of PSPACE and NPSPACE, and other space complexity classes. Then, we will explore the concept of the ‘polynomial hierarchy’, which generalises P, NP, and co-NP, and is contained within PSPACE. After that, we will delve into Boolean circuits, the ‘non-uniform’ variant of Turing machines. We will cover some classical lower bounds on Boolean circuits and discuss recent developments. After this, we will start randomization in computation. At the end, I will talk about catalytic computation, a rapidly developing research area and will conclude with a recent breakthrough of Ryan Williams, which shows that deterministic time can be ‘simulated’ by square-root space.
prerequisites_mandatory: CSE222 (can be waived if a student has a deep understanding of design and analysis of algorithms)
CSE322 (I will cover Turing machines in the first week. I will conduct a short quiz after that. If students perform well, TOC can be waived off)

outcomes.label: CO1
outcomes.raw_text: Describe different models of computation and different classes of computational problems

outcomes.label: CO2
outcomes.raw_text: Determine "reductions" between various computational problems and discuss lower bounds on various models of computation

outcomes.label: CO3
outcomes.raw_text: Discuss complete problems for different computational classes and relationships between various classes

outcomes.label: CO4
outcomes.raw_text: Explain important results and open problems in computational complexity
